utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Mr. Milovancevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Grujic, I am Defence counsel for the accused Milan Martic. Now begins the stage that is called cross-examination. I believe you're familiar with it. I would appreciate it if you could try, together with me, to make a pause between question and answers for the sake of the interpreters. In your background details you stated that you found a job with the Ministry of the Interior of Croatia in 1972. You also stated that in 1980 you went to a course where you got a diploma for traffic police.

utterances.speaker: IVAN GRUJIC
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: In your data I also read that after that you were sent to one year's special training within the police academy, where you acquired experience and qualifications for highly-skilled work within state security, and became a junior inspector; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: IVAN GRUJIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Between 1984 and 1992 you worked in the state security section of the Ministry of the Interior on jobs related to terrorism, correct?

utterances.speaker: IVAN GRUJIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: You stated that in that period you completed anti-terrorist activity training and became a post-graduate to the faculty of criminal sciences and were promoted to the rank of inspector, earning the title of a criminologist.

utterances.speaker: IVAN GRUJIC
utterances.text: Not quite. I completed this training for anti-terrorism and before that year I became a post-graduate, and the faculty of criminal science, criminological science, that was before 1990.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Can you tell us when you graduated from the criminology course and when you were promoted to inspector first class.

utterances.speaker: IVAN GRUJIC
utterances.text: As for the rank, I think I got it in 1980 -- sorry, 1998. I got my promotion in 1998 to inspector first class.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Looking at your professional background, I see that in 1990 you were appointed to the post of independent inspector, and head of the war section office of the service for the protection of constitutional order in Osijek. When exactly was it in 1990?

utterances.speaker: IVAN GRUJIC
utterances.text: I cannot tell you exactly, but it was in the first half of that year. Between March and May, if I remember correctly.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Did I understand well; it was 1990?

utterances.speaker: IVAN GRUJIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Is it true that in 1990 there was a war section of the service for the protection of constitutional order in Osijek?

utterances.speaker: IVAN GRUJIC
utterances.text: Things were a bit more complicated than that. According to the organisation that existed then, there existed certain areas covered by certain war outposts as a contingency plan, in case they have to be activated. So in that year I was indeed appointed head of such a war outpost that hadn't been activated yet.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us until when you continued to be head of that war outpost of the service of the protection of constitutional order of Osijek?

utterances.speaker: IVAN GRUJIC
utterances.text: Until the 1st of April 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Is it correct when it says that you moved to the Information Security Service when you left your previous job on the 1st of April?

utterances.speaker: IVAN GRUJIC
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us, to which ministry did this Information Security Service belong?

utterances.speaker: IVAN GRUJIC
utterances.text: I'm certain it is specified there. From the Ministry of the Interior on the 1st of April, 1992, by decision of the then minister, I was transferred to a job in the Ministry of Defence of the Republic of Croatia, under which they had this service that was named Information and Security Service.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Is it correct that from the Ministry of the Interior you transferred to the Ministry of Defence, to the Information Security Service, by virtue of an agreement between the minister of defence and the minister of interior?

utterances.speaker: IVAN GRUJIC
utterances.text: Right. I can explain very briefly what it is about. Since we were understaffed in this area, an agreement was reached between the ministries to the effect that a certain number of staff from the Ministry of the Interior would be transferred to the Ministry of Defence.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. When you speak about your transfer to the Information Security Service within the Ministry of Defence, you say that you worked as an inspector for Eastern Slavonia and that upon moving from the police to the army, you became a major.

utterances.speaker: IVAN GRUJIC
utterances.text: Yes, we have certain rules of procedure concerning such transfers and the change in rank and, according to those rules, I became major in the army.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: In your background, professional background, it is stated that the government of Croatia, by virtue of a decision from 1993, appointed you president of the Republic of Croatia's Commission for Detainees and Missing Persons.

utterances.speaker: IVAN GRUJIC
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Before this appointment in 1993, did you perform a similar job in a similar agency in 1991 to 1993?

utterances.speaker: IVAN GRUJIC
utterances.text: No. But in 1993, if that is what you're driving at, I was also appointed to a commission for war crimes of the Republic of Croatia. But that followed my appointment to the Commission for Detainees and Missing Persons.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: You say that this government office for detainees was founded in 2000, and you were appointed head of that office; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: IVAN GRUJIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: You also explained that after this office for detained and missing persons was ended in January, 1994, you were appointed assistant minister, and later, by decision of the Republic of Croatia's government in August, 2005, you were appointed commissioner for war crimes, right?

utterances.speaker: IVAN GRUJIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: When you mentioned a moment ago that you were a member of the commission for war crimes, I suppose you meant this decision of the government from 1994, appointing you.

utterances.speaker: IVAN GRUJIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: In your professional background I also read that by a decision of the president of the Republic of Croatia, in 1996 you were promoted to the rank of colonel; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: IVAN GRUJIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: As president of the government Commission for Detained and Missing Persons, which you were from 1993, I suppose you succeeded the work of two previous commissions; one commission for handling persons captured in war, and the commission for persons who went missing in the war in Croatia.

utterances.speaker: IVAN GRUJIC
utterances.text: That's correct. Two commissions merged and one commission resulted, the government's Commission for Detained and Missing Persons, attached to the government.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Therefore, could it be said that starting in 1990, when you were appointed inspector in the Ministry of the Interior of Croatia, and then in 1992 when you moved to the Ministry of Defence, to the Security and Information Service there, that since then until today you held positions described by you as a commissioner, working in various ministries of the government of Croatia?

utterances.speaker: IVAN GRUJIC
utterances.text: Your question is not quite clear to me. I submitted, as part of the documentation with my statement, the dates of each of my appointments, and from 1993 all of the appointments that were given by the government of Croatia confirmed that I was a commissioner, a civil servant. I worked in various jobs in the Ministry of the Interior until 1992, holding various functions. In 1992 I was promoted to the rank of major. I stayed there and then moved to the Ministry of Defence, and then from there I moved to the Commission for Detained and Missing Persons, and this is the area of my work since then.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: You, as a government official during that period of time, were you aware that here, at this Tribunal, there was an indictment against the accused Ivan Cermak, Mladen Markac, and Mr. Gotovina, charging the leadership of the Republic of Croatia for participation in a joint criminal enterprise which commenced with Operation Storm in August of 1995, and whose common goal was to remove permanently the Serb population from Krajina by committing crimes listed in the indictment. Are you aware of this information?

utterances.speaker: IVAN GRUJIC
utterances.text: I don't have any official information to this effect. If there are any kind of inquiries concerning my work, then, yes, I will be able to respond officially. As for the text of the indictment and legal qualifications provided therein, I can tell you nothing about it. I learned about it from the media. The indictment itself was never served on me, because nothing in my work is related to this indictment. As for the leadership of the government of Croatia being charged, most likely the indictment specifies the specific members of the Government of Croatia. That is to say, it has nothing to do with me.

utterances.speaker: MS. VALABHJI
utterances.text: Could the usher please assist us and give a copy of the indictment, the indictment I mentioned, both to the Trial Chamber and to the expert witness and the OTP. There are B/C/S copies and English copies as well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Milovancevic, your opposite number is on her feet.

utterances.speaker: MS. VALABHJI
utterances.text: Your Honour, I would just wonder about the relevance of this line of inquiry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: May I just make a comment, and I think I made this comment some time back, Mr. Milovancevic: If your opposite number stands up, it's preferable that you sit down. That's my knowledge of court etiquette here. I'm not sure about here, but that's my culture. You don't both stand up at the same time. You have an objection, Mr. Milovancevic. Your opposite number says, What is the relevance of this line of questioning? You're talking about the charge against Croatian leaders, not the person charged. Any response?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour. Right now I am verifying the credibility and impartiality of the expert witness. I will do it by way of pointing out his role as related to other proceedings before this Tribunal. You will see that there is a traditional type of conflict of interest in this case, which can challenge the role of this expert witness as an impartial expert who is supposed to provide us certain type of information. By your leave, I will show you explicitly why I believe it important for him to see the indictment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Excepting that I don't think this witness has denied having testified in other proceedings before this Tribunal. But, having said what you have said, that's fine. Ms. Valabhji.

utterances.speaker: MS. VALABHJI
utterances.text: I would only just add that the witness has already said that he doesn't know anything about this. It's in the transcript. But that's all.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: What about your objection? Are you persisting with the objection or not?

utterances.speaker: MS. VALABHJI
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. I -- I keep the objection that I raised. I just wanted to add that point to it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: And you don't have any reply to what Mr. Milovancevic said by way of answer except just that comment?

utterances.speaker: MS. VALABHJI
utterances.text: That's right, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you. Well, in the absence of any reply, much as I am still at large, you know, I still don't see the relevance, you're talking about looking for credibility or -- or verifying credibility, Mr. Milovancevic, I hope it will emerge as you go along. You may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. Paragraph 10 of the amended indictment before you, Your Honours, and before the witness, lists that the goal of the Operation Storm, which, as the Prosecution claims, was conducted by joint forces and participants in the joint criminal enterprise, was to forcibly expel all Serb population from the territory of Krajina. There is a detailed description there. If you wish, I can read it out to you, but I don't want to use up the valuable time. What is important for me is that in paragraph 12 it says that many persons took part in this joint criminal enterprise, together with the accused Cermak and Markac, and that these persons include Mr. Franjo Tudjman, president of the Republic of Croatia; Mr. Gojko Susak, minister of defence of the Republic of Croatia; Mr. Janko Bobetko, head of -- chief of the Main Staff of the Croatian army; Mr. Cervenko, Chief of Staff of the Croatian army during Operation Storm; Ante Gotovina, former officer of the Croatian army; as well as various officers, officials and members of Croatian government, and political establishment at all levels, including municipal governments and local organisations. In addition to them, also various leaders and members of the Croatian Democratic Union, various officials and members of the armed forces of the Republic of Croatia, including Croatian government, Croatian leadership, special police, civilian police, as well as other security and intelligence services of the Republic of Croatia, as well as other identified and unidentified persons.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Given that there is this indictment issued by this Office of the Prosecutor against the said accused, which also includes people from the top establishment of the Republic of Croatia, I would like to ask the expert witness whether, in the relevant period of time, he was a member of security or intelligence services and whether he served in positions mentioned by him. Yes or no.

utterances.speaker: IVAN GRUJIC
utterances.text: No. I have to clarify my position. At the time when the government appoints an official, the official in question is a civil servant. I will reserve the right, which is generally recognised in all countries, to -- to be called by their rank. This is why my rank is mentioned, that of colonel. However, I have to say that after 1993 I did not work in those positions. Rather, I performed the tasks described in the decree of the government of Croatia on establishing the Commission on Detained and Missing Persons. My tasks are listed in the decree. Later on, these responsibilities were transferred to other institutions.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. That is to say you come here to testify as the OTP expert witness, the same Office of the Prosecution that charged the top leadership of Croatia, including its government, for persecution of Serbs from Krajina. You confirmed that you were an official of that government appointed by that government, and you go on to claim that you can be impartial and honest in your testimony, when testifying about the persecution of Serbian citizens of Croatia. Do you believe that this is --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Milovancevic, I don't see where you're going with this cross-examination. The charges that you are talking about are charges of people who worked in their -- people, senior people in the government of Croatia. It has nothing to do with this person's -- this witness's responsibilities as a witness in this matter. I still want to understand where do you say there is a conflict or where you say there is -- there is no credibility.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. It is entirely clearly to me what position was held by Mr. Grujic in the government of Croatia. But he's not an eye-witness. He is an expert witness. Today he told us that all of the information he submitted to the Tribunal were provided to him by the Ministry of Defence, Ministry of the Interior, Ministry of Justice, and other ministries of the government of the Croatia. All of these ministries as integral part of the government of Croatia and the ruling government administration of Croatia, were indicted by this Office of the Prosecutor in the indictment that I gave you. This is not the first time that an expert witness, whose credibility is questionable, comes here to testify, portraying himself as an impartial, knowledgeable expert, who is supposed to assist the Trial Chamber in determining the information concerning which we ourselves are not qualified enough. I will attempt in the remaining portion of my cross-examination to show that these two issues are linked. It was important for me to have the witness confirm to us what positions were held by him, and apart from that, I have no further questions for the expert witness. I believe that this is a good time for adjournment of today's proceedings.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Just before we -- we adjourn, there is an objection on the table, and the Chamber must rule of it. I've got to understand your line of cross-examination. After this long explanation, I still don't understand what you're trying to say. The witness is testifying on events that took place long before Operation Storm. And he's -- I don't know whether he has ever testified on Operation Storm, and even if he did, that's a completely different incident. He's talking here about things that have nothing to do with Operation Storm for which these people that you mentioned in this indictment are charged. I would like to see where the conflict exists between him being a civil servant of the Croatian government and coming to testify here about allegations of attacks on Croats long before Operation Storm.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, by your leave, I will point to you to the allegations in this indictment. The Prosecution brought this expert witness here, who submitted a written report indicating that 3.400 Serbs had been expelled from Croatia. In the indictment, the Prosecution mentions a figure of several -- of tens of thousands of people. How can these figures be reconciled? How can it be reconciled that in one indictment the Prosecution alleges that tens of thousands of Serbs were expelled whereas in another indictment they mention a figure of 3.000 something? I can verify the figure for you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I still don't understand how that has anything to do with the price of butter.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This expert, Your Honours, in our view, defends the interests of the government which appointed him. He is here to conceal the action of his government, the government that was charged by the OTP indictment. Nothing what he said here corroborates the facts from the indictment against Cermak and Markac.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Milovancevic, this witness is not testifying in the case against Mladen Markac or Ivan Cermak. He is testifying in the trial of Mr. Martic. How you say he is protecting his government when his government is not on trial, I cannot understand. This is what I don't understand.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I'm just trying to see whether the doubts that the Defence has about the credibility of this witness are legitimate or not. And I'm trying to verify that by showing that the official of the government accused for -- accused of persecuting Serbs is qualified to testify now here about these other crimes. In our view, those two things cannot be reconciled; in Prosecution's view, it seems they can.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Milovancevic, if you have doubts about the credibility of the witness and you want to check whether your doubts are legitimate, you've got to lay a basis for it. You can't go on a fishing expedition. You are saying that you are going to show by asking questions from this indictment. You have read to us two paragraphs in this indictment. The Bench still doesn't see the relevance of this indictment to these proceedings, even after you have read what I would assume you regard as relevant to your questions from this document. I cannot -- or the Bench cannot allow a continued cross-examination until we see which -- where you are going. You have not laid the basis. You are having doubts about the credibility of the witness, and you want to check if your doubts are legitimate, I think you could check that when you do your preparation, and when you have done your preparation and you have a foundation for your doubts, come here and argue the witness's lack of credibility. What you are doing, you're doing exactly what I suggested you are doing; you are going on a fishing expedition to find out if your doubts are legitimate.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NOSWORTHY
utterances.text: Mr. Milovancevic, just before you go on, I would just like to say something to you. I must confess that you have left me a bit confused because you had pitched your submission or your responses to the question from the Court slightly different from how I thought it was going. I thought your submissions would be twofold; that firstly you take issue as to the impartiality of the witness, and there is a conflict of interest because of the interest on the part of the DPP in his initial instruction and briefing; and secondly, you were taking issue as to the integrity of his compilations contained in the exhibits at the end of the day, because the source was a tainted source in that it came from certain officials of Croatia who had an interest to serve and he himself had an interest to serve. Is that not what is the substance of your objections?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That is correct, Your Honour. It's just that I have been put in an uncomfortable position. Namely, I have to state my position about the objection of the opposite side, none of the arguments being specific. But all this will be clarified if I am allowed to continue this line of questioning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NOSWORTHY
utterances.text: But, strictly speaking, you do not need the indictment in order to do that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, at this moment there is no other way in which I can expose the complete disproportion of what is stated by the OTP in one indictment and the same kind of data they are producing in this case. These numbers are completely disparate, but if you allow me to continue my cross-examination, I will be able to demonstrate that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: My problem, Mr. Milovancevic, is that these are two separate incidents. Neither the OTP nor anybody has tried to suggest that these are identical and therefore numbers must be equal on either side. Obviously whatever may have happened to -- in the attacks of 1991, the people who may have died or been maimed or been detained or been deported are not going to be exact same number as the number of people who would have been involved under similar circumstances in 1995 during Operation Storm. There is no suggestion here of comparisons. You are bringing the comparisons. And the Bench is trying to find what the relevance of the comparison is. Certainly, if the Croats attacked the Serbs in 1995, they stand or fall by their deeds then, which go with the numbers that were involved in that case, which numbers will not be the same as the numbers of 1991. And to quote numbers from this indictment and want to compare them to the numbers that this witness gave when this witness has given no comparative numbers whatsoever -- he's talking about one issue, 1991 case, and he's comparing it to no other. So the Bench doesn't understand where you're going.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, in paragraphs 50, 51, 52 and 53 of the indictment before you the Office of the Prosecutor deals with certain events. I'm not comparing two indictments. I am just talking about the way facts are presented. In this indictment, and in any other indictment, the same facts relate to the same events, the same participants, the same area, the same population, the same statistics. And in any case, in this or another one or a third one, these statistics, this data should correspond. If there is a large disproportion, that gives birth to doubt. But at this moment I'm just asking the witness if he indeed occupied the positions he said he occupied in the said period. He confirmed that. Now, by comparing his expert report, in light of this indictment only, we will be able to establish whether he is or isn't an independent, impartial expert. All this are answers that are yet to come.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Can you tell the Chamber what is contained in paragraphs 50, 51, 52 and 53 of this indictment, which is presented differently? And differently from what?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, from this indictment I just excerpted certain details that should display the logical, factual, chronological connection with all that this expert is testifying to. In the course of later cross-examination I will demonstrate the essence of it. I am just trying to say that through this expert, that the OTP is trying to tell us that in the period from 1991 to 1995, in Croatia, there were 3.400 expelled Serbs - that is the essence of all the material that was produced to us by this witness - and in another indictment the same Office of the Prosecutor, speaking about the same area and about the same period, the Prosecution is telling us that the number of the expelled Serbs was in the tens of thousands. So I'm asking the question: How is that possible? It's not easy, but it's not the first time either that I'm asking this question. I raised it in several Status Conferences as well, and meetings. Now we have reached it again at this stage.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: You are saying that this witness has testified that in the period 1991 to 1995 in Croatia 3.400 Serbs were expelled? I thought this witness is testifying about the statistics of the people that were either expelled or killed or detained in the war of 1991 insofar as he has been able to ascertain. Did this witness testify in this case, Mr. Milovancevic, in this case where -- the case of Ivan Cermak and Mladen Markac?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, that case has not began yet. The trial hasn't begun. So it's my mistake; it's not 3.400, but it's 3.104 in the period from 1991 to 1995. That is the claim of this witness, and that is the claim presented by the OTP as their finding. But in a different indictment, they say that in the same period, in the same area, tens of thousands of Serbs were expelled. That's the fact that I'm trying to point out to you. In 1991-1995 period, they are giving two different figures for two different cases.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Milovancevic, I guess you do understand that people make allegations in the indictments and then they call evidence to prove their allegations. Now, the allegations in this indictment will be allegations made by the OTP. This witness here knows nothing about those allegations. He is here to testify about allegations relating to the case that this Chamber is hearing and the case that he has investigated. He tells you he doesn't -- he knows nothing about this other case. He -- where the Prosecutor may have got the figures that he -- that the Prosecutor quotes in this indictment, this witness has nothing do with. And I would imagine that even the numbers that this witness testified to this morning are not necessarily -- do not necessarily tell you, with any numbers, if any, that the Prosecutor might have given in the Martic case, because this witness just goes by the -- by his own investigations. Now, I'm sorry, I still don't understand where you're going. And I think the Chamber needs to rule on this objection at this stage. The objection is upheld. It's way beyond time to take the break. The Court will take an adjournment until tomorrow. I am told tomorrow we are starting at -- we are in Courtroom I, not Courtroom II. Court adjourned.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Tuesay, the 11th day of April, 2006, at 9.00 a.m. 24 25

procedural_notes.text: --- Whereupon the hearing adjourned at 2.04 p.m.,
